title: The Science of Teaching Choir
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: After observing a choir teacher's class, Stuart uses the lesson as a live case study for several principles from his Principles of Learning Course. He highlights the teacher's relentless use of concrete examples and non-examples to make an abstract skill, vocal articulation, clear, his practice of treating all students as novices by explicitly unpacking components like performance anxiety, breath, and posture, his use of retrieval practice, asking students to verbally recall notes given in current and prior lessons, and his use of a sports analogy to reframe strict feedback as evidence of real growth, an example of defining success. Stuart closes with two takeaways: that these learning principles apply across disciplines, not just academic subjects, and that teachers should make a habit of observing colleagues' classrooms, something he still finds inspiring nearly two decades into his own career.
points: The choir teacher's repeated use of concrete comparisons, it's not like this, it's like that, is offered as a model for making abstract skills tangible for novices.

Retrieval practice showed up organically in the choir room: the teacher had students verbally recall notes from both the current and prior lessons, reinforcing memory through recall rather than re-explanation.

The teacher's framing of tough feedback via a Detroit Lions playoff analogy, nitpicking as a sign a team or class has gotten good enough to be worth nitpicking, is highlighted as a concrete example of defining success for students.

Stuart's closing challenge is practical and simple: observe a colleague's classroom this week, arguing the learning principles that show up in choir are the same ones that show up in English, math, or any other subject.
quotes: Throughout the lesson, he didn't seek clarity for his novices just once or twice; he was relentlessly seeking clarity for his novices.

He even brought in the power of testing. After giving notes on a practiced segment, he asked the students to verbally recall the notes he had just given them. He then asked them to bring in notes he'd given on the section in prior lessons.

He likened this to how much he's seen the students grow this year, saying that his pickiness is an indicator of how far they've come, saying that his students are like the Lions in that their star is rising, they are a program on the move.

Sitting in his room, watching a regular lesson play out, was like a revelation to me. I was encouraged, challenged, inspired. There was nothing special about it — he was a regular teacher doing our regular work.

First, note how the principles of learning are as relevant to choir as they are to English as they are to what any of us do. Second, has it been a minute since you sat in on the lesson of a colleague? Do yourself a big favor: make it happen this week.
